extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students in real analysis / multivariable calculus
extracted.subtask_description: Statements, definitions, and necessary-and-sufficient criteria for Riemann integrability and related results in several real variables (partitions, upper/lower sums, measure/content zero, Fubini, change-of-variables). Intended to guide checking integrability and manipulating integrals in R^n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common refinement of partitions
rubrics_metrics.description: If P = (P1, ..., Pn) and P' = (P'1, ..., P'n) are two partitions of A, then P and P' have at least one common refinement P* = (P*1, ..., P*n); specifically, for each j, P*j may be taken to be a common refinement of Pj and P'j.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to compare upper and lower sums computed relative to different partitions; the construction of a common refinement underlies monotonicity results and comparison arguments (see Lemma 3.23 and subsequent proofs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotonicity of upper and lower sums under refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: For a bounded function f on A, if P* is a refinement of partition P then L(P,f) ≤ L(P*,f) and U(P*,f) ≤ U(P,f). Also, for any partitions P1, P2 of A, L(P1,f) ≤ U(P2,f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ordering of lower and upper sums is the basis for defining lower and upper integrals and proving existence/uniqueness of the Riemann integral; used repeatedly to sandwich integrals and in proofs (Lemma 3.23 and later).

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann integrability criterion via upper and lower sums
rubrics_metrics.description: A bounded function f on a closed rectangle A is Riemann integrable on A if and only if for each ε > 0 there exists a partition P of A with U(P,f) − L(P,f) < ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the operational test for integrability: given ε, find a partition that makes upper and lower sums arbitrarily close. Many proofs (continuity ⇒ integrable, integrability via oscillation) are carried out by constructing such partitions (Lemma 3.23e, used throughout).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity implies Riemann integrability on a closed rectangle
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : A → R is continuous on a closed rectangle A (finite, positive volume), then f is Riemann integrable on A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof uses uniform continuity (Heine–Borel Theorem) to control oscillation on small rectangles so that U(P,f)−L(P,f) is small. This is Theorem 3.24; it justifies dropping integrability hypotheses when f is continuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic and inequality properties of integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: If f1 and f2 are Riemann integrable on A then: (a) f1+f2 is integrable and ∫(f1+f2)=∫f1+∫f2; (b) scalar multiples c f1 are integrable and ∫c f1 = c ∫f1; (c) if f1 ≤ f2 then ∫f1 ≤ ∫f2; (d) compositions with continuous scalar maps: if m ≤ f1 ≤ M and φ:[m,M]→R is continuous then φ∘f1 is integrable; (e) integrability of absolute value and inequalities of integrals (e.g. |∫f| ≤ ∫|f|); (f/g) products, powers and related closure properties under reasonable hypotheses are in R(A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This collects the standard closure properties (Proposition 3.25). The textbook lists the parts (a)–(g); use them to combine, bound, and manipulate integrable functions algebraically. For products/compositions one may need additional boundedness/continuity hypotheses as given in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform limit preserves integrability and integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: If {f_n} is a sequence of Riemann integrable functions on A that converges uniformly to f on A, then f is Riemann integrable on A and lim_n ∫_A f_n = ∫_A f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows passage of limits inside integrals under uniform convergence (Theorem 3.26). The uniformity hypothesis is essential in the Riemann theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann sums criterion (convergence of Riemann sums)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition: given partition P select a sample point t_R in each component rectangle R and form S(P,{t_R},f) = Σ_R f(t_R)·vol(R). If f is Riemann integrable on A then S(P,{t_R},f) → ∫_A f dx as the mesh µ(P) → 0. Conversely, if f is bounded and there exists r such that for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 with |S(P,{t_R},f)−r| < ε whenever µ(P) < δ (for any choice of sample points), then f is Riemann integrable and ∫_A f dx = r.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reformulates integrability in terms of convergence of Riemann sums as the maximum rectangle diameter (mesh) goes to zero (Theorem 3.27). Useful for practical approximations and for verifying integrability from sampling behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oscillation and partition lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: Oscillation at x0 is osc_f(x0)=lim_{δ→0} sup_{|x−x0|<δ} |f(x)−f(x0)|. Lemma 3.31: If A is a nontrivial closed rectangle and f is bounded on A with osc_f(x) < ε for all x in A, then there exists a partition P of A with U(P,f) − L(P,f) ≤ 2ε·vol(A) (i.e., the upper−lower sums can be made small).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controlling pointwise oscillation uniformly leads to small U−L via compactness: cover by small rectangles where oscillation < ε, then take the partition generated by their endpoints (Lemma 3.31). This is the usual ‘oscillation → integrability’ step used in Theorem 3.29 proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and properties of measure zero
rubrics_metrics.description: A subset E ⊆ R^n is of measure 0 if for every ε>0 E can be covered by a finite or countably infinite set of closed rectangles of total volume < ε; equivalently one may use open rectangles. Examples/properties: singleton is measure 0, a face of a rectangle has measure 0, subsets inherit measure 0, countable unions of measure-0 sets have measure 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This notion is used to characterize integrability (Theorem 3.29). The text contrasts measure zero with 'content 0' (finite covering only) and gives the rational points in [0,1] as a set of measure 0 but not content 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content zero and relation to measure zero
rubrics_metrics.description: A bounded set E has content 0 if for every ε>0 E can be covered by a finite set of closed rectangles of total volume < ε. Every set of content 0 has measure 0. Lemma 3.30: if E is compact and of measure 0 then E has content 0. The converse need not hold for noncompact/countable-cover cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content 0 is a convenient finite-cover notion used in compactness arguments. The distinction matters (rationals in [0,1] have measure 0 but not content 0). Lemma 3.30 justifies finite coverings for compact measure-0 sets in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrability characterized by discontinuities having measure zero (Lebesgue's criterion for Riemann integrability in R^n)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 3.29: Let A be a finite closed rectangle in R^n and f : A → R a bounded function. Then f is Riemann integrable on A if and only if the set B = { x ∈ A : f is not continuous at x } has measure 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the key necessary-and-sufficient condition (often called Lebesgue's criterion) used to decide integrability by locating discontinuities. The proof uses oscillation, partitions, and content/measure-zero coverings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fubini's Theorem for the Riemann integral
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 3.32: Let A ⊆ R^m and B ⊆ R^n be closed rectangles and f : A×B → R be Riemann integrable. For x ∈ A let f_x(y)=f(x,y) (as a function on B). Then the lower and upper integrals L(f_x), U(f_x) are integrable on A and ∫_{A×B} f = ∫_A (∫_B f(x,y) dy) dx (and similarly exchanging the order). Corollary 3.33: If f is continuous on A×B then the iterated integrals equal the double integral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Fubini to compute double integrals as iterated integrals when hypotheses are met. The text warns about Riemann pathologies (restriction of an integrable f need not be integrable in one variable for each fixed other variable) and points out the Lebesgue integral removes such pathologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change-of-variables formula under C^1 diffeomorphism (with compact support hypothesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 3.34 (preliminary R^n change-of-variables): Let φ be one-one of class C^1 from open U ⊆ R^n onto φ(U) with det φ'(x) nowhere 0. For every continuous f on φ(U) whose support is a compact subset of φ(U), ∫_{φ(U)} f(y) dy = ∫_U f(φ(x)) |det φ'(x)| dx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires φ to be a C^1 diffeomorphism (locally invertible everywhere) and f to be continuous with compact support in φ(U) (the compact-support hypothesis avoids boundary issues mentioned in polar-coordinate examples). The text explains proof strategy: decompose φ locally into flips and primitive maps, use Fubini and 1-D change-of-variables, and patch via partition of unity. This theorem is declared preliminary; more general forms are proved later with Lebesgue theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local factorization of a C^1 map near a point (nonlinear column/row reduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma 3.35: Suppose φ is C^1 in a neighborhood of 0 with φ(0)=0 and φ'(0) invertible. Then on some neighborhood of 0, φ factors as a composition β1 ◦ ... ◦ β_{i-1} ◦ √_1 ◦ ... ◦ √_n where each β_j is either a flip or the identity and each √_j is a primitive C^1 map (one nontrivial entry) with invertible derivative at 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lemma provides the local decomposition used in the change-of-variables proof: primitive mappings handle nonlinear row operations, flips handle coordinate exchanges; together they replicate a nonlinear analogue of matrix factorization so local Jacobians multiply correctly and one can reduce to 1-D and Fubini steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of partitions of unity to paste local change-of-variables results
rubrics_metrics.description: When φ factors locally and the change-of-variables formula is established on each local piece (for functions supported inside that piece), a finite partition of unity subordinate to a finite cover of the compact support allows summing local results to obtain the global formula for f (Theorem 3.34 proof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard patching device: construct finitely many C^∞ (or C^1 here) functions summing to 1 on the compact support, each supported in a region where φ behaves as needed; apply the local formula to each term and sum.
